title: The one-step Ex comparison is a weak homotopy equivalence
statement: Use simplicial sets [def-weil-pbc-simplicial-set] and weak homotopy equivalences defined by geometric realization [def-cbc-enhanced-diagrams-cones]. For $n\geq0$, let $\mathcal P_+([n])$ be the poset of nonempty subsets of $[n]$ ordered by inclusion, and define $(\operatorname{Ex}X)_n=\operatorname{Hom}(N(\mathcal P_+([n])),X)$, with operators given by images of subsets under monotone maps. The map $\lambda_n:N(\mathcal P_+([n]))\to\Delta^n$ is induced by $S\mapsto\max S$. The natural comparison $j_X:X\to\operatorname{Ex}X$ sends an $n$-simplex $\sigma:\Delta^n\to X$ to $\sigma\circ\lambda_n$. For every small simplicial set $X$, $j_X$ is a weak homotopy equivalence: $|j_X|$ induces a bijection on path components and an isomorphism on every homotopy group at every basepoint of $|X|$.

source.place: Theorem 3.3.5.1 (00Z2), with the comparison map of Construction 3.3.4.3 (Kerodon tag, not a Stacks tag; no Stacks result supplies this simplicial homotopy theorem). Online source read 2026-10-17; archive WANTED.

proof.text: Write $[A,B]_{\mathrm e}$ for maps modulo the equivalence relation generated by edges in $\operatorname{Fun}(A,B)$, as in [lem-cbc-realization-weak-equivalence]. Precomposition and postcomposition act on these classes: compose each edge homotopy with the fixed map. On simplices, $\operatorname{Ex}(u)$ is postcomposition by $u$, so it respects identities and composites. For a monotone $\alpha:[m]\to[n]$, $\alpha(\max S)=\max\alpha(S)$; therefore the subset-image operators commute with the last-vertex maps and $j$ is natural: $\operatorname{Ex}(u)j_A=j_Bu$. Ex also preserves the edge-generated homotopy relation, with an explicit formula: if $H:A\times\Delta^1\to B$ is a homotopy, send an $n$-simplex $(\sigma,t)$ of $\operatorname{Ex}A\times\Delta^1$, where $\sigma:\operatorname{Sd}\Delta^n\to A$ and $t:[n]\to[1]$, to $H\circ(\sigma,\Delta(t)\lambda_n):\operatorname{Sd}\Delta^n\to B$. Naturality of $\lambda_n$ makes this a simplicial map into $\operatorname{Ex}B$. At $t=0,1$ its restrictions are $\operatorname{Ex}(H|_0),\operatorname{Ex}(H|_1)$. Applying this to each edge in a zigzag defines $[u]\mapsto[\operatorname{Ex}(u)]$.

source.place: Theorem 3.3.5.1, functoriality and naturality in its diagram; the agent writes the homotopy-preservation formula explicitly.

proof.text: Fix a Kan complex $Y$ in the same universe. For every small simplicial set $T$, [lem-coef-subdivision-last-vertex-equivalence] and the implication (i) to (ii) of [lem-cbc-realization-weak-equivalence] give a bijection $[T,Y]_{\mathrm e}\to[\operatorname{Sd}T,Y]_{\mathrm e}$, $[f]\mapsto[f\lambda_T]$. The homotopy adjunction of [lem-coef-subdivision-ex-homotopy-adjunction] gives a bijection from the latter set to $[T,\operatorname{Ex}Y]_{\mathrm e}$. By the last-vertex/transpose correspondence in [lem-coef-subdivision-face-poset-calculus], the transpose of $f\lambda_T$ is $j_Yf$ (on an $n$-simplex $\sigma$ it is $f\sigma\lambda_n$). Hence postcomposition $[j_Y]_*:[T,Y]_{\mathrm e}\to[T,\operatorname{Ex}Y]_{\mathrm e}$ is bijective for every $T$.

source.place: Proposition 3.3.5.7 (00Z7), mapping-class reduction using 00YZ and 00Z6; 03X7 identifies realization weak equivalences with the testing criterion.

proof.text: Take $T=\operatorname{Ex}Y$ in Step 2. Surjectivity gives a representative $r:\operatorname{Ex}Y\to Y$ with $[j_Yr]=[1]$. Precomposing this equality by $j_Y$ gives $[j_Yrj_Y]=[j_Y]$. Injectivity in Step 2 for $T=Y$ then gives $[rj_Y]=[1]$. For every $A$, postcomposition by $r$ is consequently inverse to postcomposition by $j_Y$ on edge-generated homotopy classes. This argument uses only composition of representatives and composition of the finite homotopy zigzags; no choice of a strict inverse or equality of simplicial maps is claimed.

source.place: Proposition 3.3.5.7, elementary representable-functor argument expanded to an inverse on homotopy classes.

proof.text: For a finite poset $Q$, write $\operatorname{Ch}(Q)$ for its poset of nonempty chains, ordered by inclusion. The finite-poset identifications of [lem-coef-subdivision-face-poset-calculus] identify $\operatorname{Sd}^2NQ$ with $N\operatorname{Ch}(\operatorname{Ch}(Q))$. On a vertex $\mathcal C=\{C_0\subsetneq\cdots\subsetneq C_r\}$ define $a(\mathcal C)=\{\max C_0,\ldots,\max C_r\}$ and $b(\mathcal C)=C_r$. These are chains in $Q$, are monotone in $\mathcal C$, and $a(\mathcal C)\subseteq b(\mathcal C)$. Thus $(0,\mathcal C)\mapsto a(\mathcal C)$, $(1,\mathcal C)\mapsto b(\mathcal C)$ defines a monotone map $[1]\times\operatorname{Ch}(\operatorname{Ch}(Q))\to\operatorname{Ch}(Q)$: in a mixed inequality, $a(\mathcal C)\subseteq b(\mathcal C)\subseteq b(\mathcal D)$. Taking its nerve gives $h_Q:\Delta^1\times\operatorname{Sd}^2NQ\to\operatorname{Sd}NQ$, since a chain in a product poset is a pair of chains. The face-poset formulas identify its endpoints with $\operatorname{Sd}(\lambda_{NQ})$ and $\lambda_{\operatorname{Sd}NQ}$, respectively. Images of chains and maxima commute with monotone maps, including ones identifying vertices, so $h_Q$ is natural in such maps.

source.place: Proposition 3.3.5.8 (00Z8), the two monotone maps on chains and their pointwise inclusion; finite-poset homotopy expanded by the agent.

proof.text:
For each $n$ and $\sigma:\operatorname{Sd}\Delta^n\to X$, write $\widehat\sigma:\Delta^n\to\operatorname{Ex}X$ for its adjoint and form
$$\operatorname{Sd}^2(\Delta^1\times\Delta^n)\longrightarrow\operatorname{Sd}^2\Delta^1\times\operatorname{Sd}^2\Delta^n\xrightarrow{\ell\times1}\Delta^1\times\operatorname{Sd}^2\Delta^n\xrightarrow{h_{[n]}}\operatorname{Sd}\Delta^n\xrightarrow{\sigma}X,$$
where the first map is the pair induced by projections and $\ell=\lambda_{\Delta^1}\lambda_{\operatorname{Sd}\Delta^1}$. Twice transposing by [lem-coef-subdivision-face-poset-calculus] gives $\Delta^1\times\Delta^n\to\operatorname{Ex}^2X$. The formula is natural in the simplex operators of $\sigma$, by Step 4 and naturality of $\lambda$, so these maps define a homotopy $\Delta^1\times\operatorname{Ex}X\to\operatorname{Ex}^2X$: on an $m$-simplex $(t,\sigma)$ evaluate the transposed map for $n=m$ at $(t,\mathrm{id}_{[m]})$. The double adjoint of $j_{\operatorname{Ex}X}\widehat\sigma$ is $\sigma\operatorname{Sd}(\lambda_{\Delta^n})$: its first adjoint is $\widehat\sigma\lambda_{\Delta^n}$, and transposing once more precomposes $\sigma$ with $\operatorname{Sd}(\lambda_{\Delta^n})$. This is the constructed endpoint at $0$. For the other endpoint, the first adjoint of $\operatorname{Ex}(j_X)\widehat\sigma$ is $j_X\sigma$. Its adjoint is $\sigma\lambda_{\operatorname{Sd}\Delta^n}$, since on every simplex $\tau:\Delta^m\to\operatorname{Sd}\Delta^n$ the transpose of $j_X\sigma$ is $\sigma\tau\lambda_{\Delta^m}$, exactly the colimit formula for $\sigma\lambda_{\operatorname{Sd}\Delta^n}$. This is the constructed endpoint at $1$. Hence $[j_{\operatorname{Ex}X}]=[\operatorname{Ex}(j_X)]$.

source.place: Proposition 3.3.5.8 (00Z8), double-transpose construction; the source endpoint identification is checked explicitly.

proof.text:
Fix again a Kan target $Y$ and consider $u:[\operatorname{Ex}X,Y]_{\mathrm e}\to[X,Y]_{\mathrm e}$ given by precomposition with $j_X$. For a map $f:X\to Y$, Step 3 supplies a class $[g]$ with $[j_Yg]=[\operatorname{Ex}(f)]$. Naturality gives $[j_Ygj_X]=[\operatorname{Ex}(f)j_X]=[j_Yf]$, and Step 3's injectivity for source $X$ gives $[gj_X]=[f]$. Thus $u$ is surjective. If $[gj_X]=[g'j_X]$, Step 1 permits applying Ex to this equality. Step 5 and naturality give
$$[\operatorname{Ex}(gj_X)]=[\operatorname{Ex}(g)\operatorname{Ex}(j_X)]=[\operatorname{Ex}(g)j_{\operatorname{Ex}X}]=[j_Yg],$$
and the same equation for $g'$. Injectivity of postcomposition by $j_Y$ for source $\operatorname{Ex}X$ gives $[g]=[g']$. Thus $u$ is also injective.

source.place: Theorem 3.3.5.1 (00Z2), diagram chase; surjectivity and injectivity expanded using the earlier steps.

proof.text: The argument of Step 6 applies to every Kan complex $Y$ in the universe of $X$. Condition (ii) of [lem-cbc-realization-weak-equivalence] therefore holds for $v=j_X$. Its implication (ii) to (i) proves precisely that $|j_X|$ is bijective on path components and induces isomorphisms on all based homotopy groups, as asserted. No fibrancy or nonemptiness hypothesis has been imposed on $X$.
